title: U.S. House · California's 31st District
area: The San Gabriel Valley in Los Angeles County, including areas of North Orange County. District lines were redrawn for the 2026 election under California Proposition 50.

context.text: California redrew its congressional district lines for the 2026 election cycle after voters approved Proposition 50 on November 4, 2025, a mid-decade redistricting measure.
Incumbent Democrat Gil Cisneros and Republican Eric Ching, a former city council member and mayor, advanced from the June 2, 2026 top-two primary.

summary.text: Gil Cisneros is the Democratic incumbent for California's 31st Congressional District. A Navy veteran and former Frito-Lay logistics manager, he later became a philanthropist, served one term in the U.S. House from 2019 to 2021, and was Under Secretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness from 2021. He returned to the House after the November 2024 election and serves on the Armed Services and Small Business committees.

background.text: Born in Los Angeles, California, in 1971. His official biography says he grew up in Southern California and enlisted in the U.S. Navy in 1989 after graduating from high school.

Received a Naval ROTC scholarship through the Broadened Opportunity for Officer Selection and Training Program and was commissioned an officer in 1994; Ballotpedia lists his service as a Navy supply officer from 1994 to 2004. Earned a bachelor's degree in political science from George Washington University in 1994, an MBA from Regis University in 2002, and a master's degree in urban education policy from Brown University in 2015.

Worked as a logistics manager for Frito-Lay. After winning the lottery in 2010, he and his wife Jacki established the Gilbert & Jacki Cisneros Foundation, which funds scholarships and college access programs.
In 2015 he founded the Cisneros Hispanic Leadership Institute at George Washington University, which provides scholarships for Latino students, according to his official biography.

Elected to the U.S. House from California's 39th District in 2018, and served on the Armed Services and Veterans' Affairs committees. He lost re-election in 2020 to Young Kim, and served in the House from 2019 to 2021.

Appointed Under Secretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness by President Biden in April 2021, and sworn in on August 24, 2021 after Senate confirmation. In April 2022 the Secretary of Defense named him the Pentagon's first Chief Diversity and Inclusion Officer.

Elected in November 2024 to represent California's 31st District, taking office in 2025. His committee assignments are Armed Services (Intelligence and Special Operations and Military Personnel subcommittees) and Small Business (ranking member of the Contracting and Infrastructure Subcommittee).

Co-founded the Military Transition Assistance Pathway (MTAP) Caucus and co-chairs the Military Mental Health Caucus, according to his official pages. The U.S. Navy Memorial and the Navy Supply Corps Foundation have recognized his service.

priorities.text: Says everyone deserves access to affordable, quality healthcare, and cites his work in Congress and as Under Secretary of Defense to expand healthcare access for working families.
Says he is a vocal advocate for keeping immigrant families together and protecting the pathway to citizenship.
Says the district's small businesses and entrepreneurs need an economy that works for everyone, and cites his seat on the House Committee on Small Business.

positions.summary: Led a letter urging Republican leadership not to obstruct legislation protecting Dreamers from deportation and work-authorization lapses, and has cosponsored the American Dream and Promise Act.
positions.quote: This failure of leadership is forcing Dreamers out of the workforce and placing them at risk of deportation. It is cruel and unjust, and it needs to end now.

positions.summary: Voted for legislation to restore Affordable Care Act premium tax credits, saying the credits give relief to Americans facing high healthcare costs.
positions.quote: Today, I proudly voted yes on the clean bill to restore the ACA tax credits, because we need these cost-saving tax credits to give relief to the millions of Americans feeling crushed by the weight of healthcare costs.

positions.summary: Introduced legislation citing the need for small-business relief from the administration's tariffs, which he described as chaotic.
positions.quote: I hear it every day, small businesses need relief from Trump’s chaotic use of tariffs, but the Small Business Administration Office of Advocacy, which should advocate for small businesses across the federal government, ignores them.

record.text: Serves on the House Committee on Armed Services (Intelligence and Special Operations Subcommittee; Military Personnel Subcommittee) and the House Committee on Small Business (Contracting and Infrastructure Subcommittee; Oversight, Investigations, and Regulations Subcommittee) in the 119th Congress (2025-2026).
Introduced the Streamlining Small Business Contracts Act, which would raise the threshold for single-source SBA contracts to reflect current costs and inflation.

Introduced the Cut the Burden, Keep the Benefits Act, which would require the SBA Office of Advocacy to solicit and report on small-business concerns about government actions including tariffs and healthcare rules.

candidates.name: Eric Ching
candidates.currentRole: Former city council member and two-time mayor

summary.text: Eric Ching is the Republican nominee for California's 31st Congressional District. Born in Taipei, Taiwan, he immigrated to the United States in 1982, started his own business, and has served on the Walnut city council, including as mayor. He ran unsuccessfully for the U.S. House in California's 38th District in 2022 and 2024.

background.text: Born in Taipei, Taiwan. According to his Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey, he immigrated to the United States in 1982 at age 15 with limited English, and his first job was washing dishes.

Graduated from Alhambra High School and earned a bachelor's degree from California State University, Los Angeles in 1995. He says he studied marketing and opened his own company in his early 20s; Ballotpedia lists his profession as entrepreneur and notes work as an IT professional.

Says he served on the Walnut city council for over a decade and twice as mayor, and that the city was ranked among the best to live in, was financially sound, and had over 200% in reserves when he left office.
Ran for Congress in California's 38th District in 2022 and 2024 as a Republican, losing the general election to Rep. Linda Sánchez both times.

Describes himself as a Christian and says that after his wife died in 2017 he raised his two daughters alone. Ballotpedia lists affiliations with the Wanyu Foundation, Pastor Prayer Network, and City Blessing Church.

priorities.text: Lists three key campaign messages: promoting and defending the Constitution, working to keep communities safe, and working to boost the economy.

Says his policy focus areas are community safety, the economy, and foreign relations, and that he supports parental rights and opposes what he calls indoctrination in schools in favor of STEM and "useful skills."

positions.summary: Says on his campaign website that he supports the right to keep and bear arms.
positions.quote: I will support our rights to keep and bear arms.

researchNotes: Gil Cisneros has not completed Ballotpedia's 2026 Candidate Connection survey; positions and priorities were drawn from his official House issues pages and press releases. His federal floor votes and FEC totals are added separately by script. Eric Ching completed the 2026 survey and a separate quote from his campaign website, which are the basis for his priorities and the gun-rights position listed here. The 'guns' issue key in this guide is phrased as support for stricter gun laws, so a stated support for gun rights is recorded as 'opposes' that statement. Biography notes: Ching's Walnut city council tenure and mayoral years could not be confirmed from a loaded official source, so only his own survey account is used; Ballotpedia does not list his offices held. Corrected Cisneros's summary, which said he returned to Congress in 2023 (he took office in 2025).
